summary: For children aged 5–8, teach modelling as a design-thinking tool: a sketch, drawing, or physical model is a way to show and reason about HOW the shape or structure of a design helps it do its job, not a decorative picture. Anchor every model to a given problem, make the form–function link explicit ('how does that shape help it work?'), and let children iterate — change a shape, re-check, and re-explain. Use real objects whose form obviously serves a function as worked examples, and have children annotate features with their purpose.
misconceptions: Treating the model as a picture to make pretty rather than a tool to show how a design works.
Not connecting the model to the problem it is meant to solve.
Being unable to say WHY a chosen shape helps the object function.
Thinking any shape will do — that form and function are unrelated.
Believing a model must look exactly like the finished object rather than illustrate the key idea.
Seeing the first sketch as final rather than something to test and improve.

activities.title: Shape Shop: build and test a shelter
steps: Read/hear the given problem: 'Design a shelter that keeps the toy animals DRY in the rain.'
Assemble a shelter from choosable parts — a base, walls, and a roof you can shape as flat, domed, or sloped — drawing or placing your solution.

Run a rain check: on a flat roof, watch whether water sits and pools (and, if the roof has gaps or leaks, drips through onto the animals); reshape the roof into a slope that overhangs the walls and run the rain again to see whether the water runs off the edge and away from the animals.
Try a stability challenge too: give a tall tower a narrow base, test it with a gentle nudge (it may wobble or topple), then widen the base and re-test to compare.
Label your finished design with why each shape helps, e.g. 'the roof is sloped so the rain runs off.'
activities.insight: It was not a fancier roof that kept the animals dry — it was the SHAPE: a slope sends water away, and a wide base helps keep a structure from tipping. Form does functional work, and a model lets you show and improve how a design works.

activities.title: Shape detectives: real objects whose shape has a job
steps: Explore real objects whose shape serves a function — a boat's pointed hull, an umbrella's dome, a spoon's scoop.

For each, tap or point to the key shape-feature and reveal/say 'this shape helps because…' (the point cuts through water; the dome makes rain run off its edges, away from the person underneath; the scoop holds liquid).
Build vocabulary by naming the feature and the function it serves.
Then take your turn: pick a problem and start your own model, carrying over the 'this shape helps because…' move.
activities.insight: The shapes of made objects around us are usually chosen on purpose: the form of a designed object is tied to the function it serves, and you can read a design by asking what each shape is for.

activities.title: Design a squirrel-proof bird feeder (make-and-explain)
steps: Take the problem: birds keep eating from the feeder, but so do the squirrels. Design a feeder birds can use but squirrels can't reach the food in.
On paper or with simple materials, sketch or build a quick model of your idea.
Point to the specific shape or structural feature that stops the squirrels (e.g. a narrow perch, a dome, or a baffle) and explain how that feature does the job.
Relate your model back to the real feeder and the real squirrels.
Raise the challenge: a squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work? Change it and re-explain if needed.
activities.insight: A good model foregrounds the working feature and can be justified by how its shape solves the problem, and it adapts when the challenge gets harder — the model shows how a design works, not just what it looks like.

activities.title: Match the shape to its job (check of understanding)
steps: Look at pairs of shapes and the jobs they might do, and match each shape to the function it serves.
Given a problem, choose which of several shapes would best solve it (e.g. which roof would keep rain out).
Sort shapes into 'good for this job' and 'poor for this job' for a stated purpose, and say why.
activities.insight: You can recognise which shapes suit which functions and give a shape-based reason for the match.

activities.title: Inventor coach: talk through your design
steps: Share a design you have already drawn or built with an 'inventor' partner (adult or in-role character).
Answer prompts: 'How does that shape help it work?' and 'Which part solves the problem?'
Explain each chosen feature and refine your words until the form–function reason is clear.
activities.insight: Putting the form–function reasoning into words sharpens it and prepares you to communicate how your design works to others.

checkQuestion: Here's the problem: birds keep eating from the feeder, but so do the squirrels. Design a bird feeder that birds can use but squirrels can't reach the food in. Make a sketch or build a quick model of your idea, and show me how the shape of your design keeps the squirrels out. (Give paper/materials, set the problem, and watch what the child draws or builds and how they explain it.)
checkAnswer: The child produces a sketch or model whose SHAPE or structure does functional work — e.g. a narrow perch or a dome/baffle that a squirrel can't get past — and explains how that specific feature solves the problem, relating the model back to the real feeder and the squirrels.
